mercy_translation.text:
Perhaps they, unable to fight against things so evident, will not deny what is written but will insist that these things are still expected and that God the Word has not yet come. They repeat this constantly without blushing at their shameless opposition to what is visible.

But on this matter above all they will be refuted—not by us, but by the wisest Daniel, who indicates both the present time and the divine coming of the Savior, saying: “Seventy weeks are determined upon your people and upon the holy city, to bring sin to completion, to seal sins, to wipe away lawlessness, to make atonement for lawlessness, to bring everlasting righteousness, to seal vision and prophet, and to anoint the Holy of Holies. And you shall know and understand from the going forth of the word to answer and to rebuild Jerusalem until Christ the Ruler.”

Perhaps in other passages they can invent excuses and postpone what is written into some future time. But what can they say in response to these words, or how can they face them at all? Here Christ is explicitly indicated; the One anointed is proclaimed not simply as a human being but as the Holy of Holies; Jerusalem remains established until his coming, and thereafter prophet and vision cease in Israel.

David, Solomon, and Hezekiah were anointed long ago, yet Jerusalem and the place still remained, and prophets continued to prophesy: Gad, Asaph, Nathan, and after them Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, and others. Moreover, those anointed persons were called holy human beings, not the Holy of Holies.

If they point to the captivity and say that because of it Jerusalem did not exist, what will they say concerning the prophets? For even when the people were taken down to Babylon, Daniel and Jeremiah were there, while Ezekiel, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius interprets Daniel's seventy weeks christologically and links them to the cessation of prophecy and the status of Jerusalem.
This chapter reflects a patristic Christian-Jewish polemical setting and should be presented with historical context rather than used to denigrate Jewish people or Judaism.
